analysis.one_liner: Bars leasing of federal land with low or no oil and gas potential to end speculative leasing.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee in May 2023, received a subcommittee hearing in July 2023, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Bureau of Land Management to assess each parcel's actual oil and gas potential before offering it for lease, and to stop offering parcels rated as having low or no development potential. The bill's own findings say the government regularly leases such land at minimum bids, it rarely produces oil or gas, and taxpayers get minimal revenue while the leases block other uses like recreation and grazing. It allows exceptions for land next to producing wells and a strict variance process, with public comment required.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and users of public land. The bill targets land the government leases for near-minimum bids that rarely produces anything, so ending those leases saves the cost of issuing and managing them, frees the land for recreation, grazing, wildlife, and other uses, and reduces speculative lock-ups of public acreage. Local communities that depend on outdoor recreation and ranching also benefit from fewer dormant leases restricting multiple-use management.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Bureau of Land Management to complete an assessment of each parcel's oil and gas development potential before offering land for lease, so land with low or no potential cannot be offered for lease [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings state that low- and no-potential land is frequently leased at or near the minimum bid, rarely produces oil or gas, and yields minimal revenue for taxpayers, while the government spends resources issuing and managing those leases [S3].

The bill says leases on low- and no-potential land limit other economically valuable uses of the land, including recreation, grazing, timber, and wildlife habitat, and requires public notice and comment periods of at least 60 days on the assessments and variance requests [S3].
The bill keeps existing multiple-use and environmental review requirements intact and allows exceptions for land near producing wells to prevent drainage, so genuine production is not blocked [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that acquire cheap leases on low-potential federal land for speculation, resale, or stockpiling acreage would lose that opportunity. The government would also spend more on detailed development assessments and updates of the scenarios that guide leasing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Speculative oil and gas lease buyers

drawbacks.text: Any restriction on offering federal land for lease can be criticized as reducing domestic oil and gas supply, though the bill states its policy is not detrimental to US energy security and preserves leasing on land with real development potential [S3].

The bill adds new analytical steps, mandatory public comment periods, and 15-year update cycles for development scenarios, which would slow and raise the cost of the leasing program, a burden on the agency and on operators waiting for leases [S3].

The variance process is deliberately strict, limiting applicants to one variance per five years and capping variance parcels at 1,280 acres adjacent to producing land, which critics would call an impractical bottleneck for legitimate edge-case projects [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: stop handing out cheap leases on land that almost certainly holds no recoverable oil or gas, at the cost of more agency analysis and slower leasing paperwork. The energy cost appears small because genuinely promising land stays open to leasing; the main honest objection is added delay and administrative burden in the leasing process.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, got a subcommittee hearing, and never advanced to a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Catherine Cortez Masto introduced the bill on May 16, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S1] [S5].
On July 12, 2023, the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Subcommittee on Public Lands, Forests, and Mining held a hearing on the bill, with a printed hearing record [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee markup or a vote in either chamber and expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies that buy cheap leases on low-potential federal land are better off, since they can keep acquiring and holding speculative leases on public acreage. The lands' other users, including recreation and grazing interests, did not gain the clearer access the bill would have provided.

for.name: Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restrict leasing of low- and no-potential federal land and sought a hearing for it.

for.name: Senate Subcommittee on Public Lands, Forests, and Mining
for.role: Subcommittee of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on July 12, 2023.

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Sen. Joe Manchin, D-WV)
against.what_they_did: Took no further action after the subcommittee hearing; never scheduled a markup or advanced the bill, so it never reached the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and it never reached a vote, so no partisan alignment can be measured from the record.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and speculators
industries.note: The bill ends the ability to acquire leases at minimum bids on federal land with little or no oil and gas potential, land that is often held speculatively rather than developed. Removing those cheap leases frees public land for other uses that ordinary people enjoy.

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation, grazing, and timber users of public land
industries.note: The bill says dormant leases on low-potential land limit recreation, grazing, wildlife habitat, and timber uses, so ending those leases would free the land for these activities. It locks in multiple-use management as the stated policy.
